import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Factorial primes

A factorial prime is a prime that is one more or one less than a factorial. It
is conjectured that there are infinitely many factorial primes.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Factorial prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorial_prime)
- [OEIS A088054](https://oeis.org/A088054)
-/

namespace FactorialPrime

/-- A factorial prime is a prime one above or one below a factorial. -/
def IsFactorialPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ ∃ n : ℕ, p = n.factorial + 1 ∨ n.factorial = p + 1

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem seven_isFactorialPrime : IsFactorialPrime 7 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 3, Or.inl ?_⟩
  norm_num

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem twentyThree_isFactorialPrime : IsFactorialPrime 23 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 4, Or.inr ?_⟩
  norm_num

/-- There are infinitely many factorial primes. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinitely_many_factorial_primes :
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | IsFactorialPrime p} := by
  sorry

end FactorialPrime

reformulations.difference: The source describes the minus branch as p = n! − 1; Lean uses n.factorial = p + 1 instead.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For every natural n, Nat.factorial_pos gives 1 ≤ n.factorial, so n.factorial = p + 1 iff p = n.factorial − 1, even with truncated natural subtraction. Keeping the primality condition and plus branch unchanged therefore gives exactly the source's predicate. This pointwise equivalence was proved in Review.isFactorialPrime_source_iff in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

review.notes: Checked the definition, both test theorems, and the infinitude conjecture. Wikipedia explicitly conjectures infinitely many factorial primes of either sign, matching the statement and its open status. The tests correctly establish 7 = 3! + 1 and 23 = 4! − 1 and have no sorry dependencies. The scratch file compiles successfully: it checks small factorial candidates, excludes 0, 1 and 11, includes 2, 3, 5, 7 and 23, and proves the full infinitude statement equivalent to the usual unboundedness formulation. Allowing n = 0 introduces no extra prime because 0! = 1!. OEIS's website returned browser challenges; its complete entry was read through the official data mirror.
